not absent for mental health care and was home in bed with the flu

didn't match Talarico's schedule
. It also reviewed visual evidence, which it did not publish, 
that Talarico was at his Austin home every day of his flu
. Snopes, PolitiFact and FactCheck.org each rated or answered the claim as false or "No." One caveat is that the facility told the Daily Wire it

clusters.verdict_basis:
The 2021 committee remarks that Talarico's critics cite were about sexes, not genders. 
He said "modern science recognizes that there are many more than two biological sexes – in fact, there are six."
 
The Texas Tribune describes this as referring to people with chromosomal variations.
 LGBTQ Nation's fact check rated the "six genders" wording Half True because 
he said there are six sexes, referring to intersex chromosome variations, not six genders.
 Later he told Fox News, 
"There are not six sexes. There are two."
 Several outlets and partisan sources paraphrase the remark as "six genders" (TIME, The Federalist, the RNC chair). I found no record of him using the word "genders" with the number six. The claim swaps "genders" for "sexes", so it misstates what he said, even though he did argue that sex and gender are not binary.

clusters.text: James Talarico thinks tax dollars should pay for sex changes for kids.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim rests on Talarico's 2023 vote against SB 14, which banned gender-transition treatments for minors and barred public funding for them. 
The Dallas Morning News spot check says he did vote against the bill, but a no vote doesn't by itself show he supported taxpayer-funded surgeries for minors.
 
PolitiFact (via the Houston Chronicle) found no evidence that he backed any legislation using taxpayer money for gender-reassignment surgery
, and it rated a near-identical ad claim False. 
CNN reports that he also voted for failed amendments that would have limited the ban to surgeries while leaving hormone therapy and puberty blockers allowed
. 
FactCheck.org reports that his campaign says he opposes gender-reassignment surgery for minors, and that he told Fox News he would "absolutely" support a national ban on such surgery for minors.
 The claim turns a vote against a broad bill into an affirmative position on "sex changes for kids" paid for with taxpayer money, and the records don't show that position.

clusters.text: A Lindner Center of Hope employee or psychiatric hospital said James Talarico was recently discharged.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim comes from an Oct. 11 X post by Nick Sortor and Rhein Amacher. It included an audio recording of a woman who said she was at the Lindner Center of Hope and that Talarico was just discharged. 
Amacher wrote that the caller identified herself as a female facility employee and said Talarico had been discharged within the previous 24–48 hours.

clusters.text: James Talarico said parents who do not transition their kids are abusive.
clusters.verdict_basis: The 2019 hearing on HB 1910 is the source of the claim. Fox News and others report that Talarico, speaking on that bill, said denying a child's gender identity is "incredibly harmful" and that "whether or not we label it with the term abuse, it's abusive for sure." The bill would have barred courts from weighing a parent's refusal to acknowledge a child's gender identity in custody cases. That is not the same as saying parents "who do not transition their kids" are abusive. The comment concerned refusing to acknowledge or affirm gender identity, and the reports I found do not show him mentioning medical or social transition. He also hedged on the legal label, saying he opposed ruling it out as abuse. His campaign says he supports parental rights, and a Texas PAC ad claiming he backs jailing such parents was found unsupported by his legislative record. The claim is therefore a compressed, overstated version of a real quote. It also leaves out that the quote is from 2019. Reporting also notes he voted against the 2025 bill (HB 1106) that excluded refusal to affirm from the legal definition of abuse. clusters.text: Ken Paxton was impeached by his own party.
clusters.verdict_basis:
On May 27, 2023, the Texas House impeached Paxton 121-23. 
Speaker Dade Phelan and 59 other Republicans joined 61 Democrats, and all 23 "no" votes came from Republicans.
 That makes 60 Republicans in favor. The impeachment began with a 
Republican-led House General Investigating Committee
, which 
voted unanimously to send the articles to the full House
. So the House did impeach him, and Republican-led bodies and many Republican members drove it. But the claim leaves out several things. The vote was bipartisan, and Democrats supplied about half of the "yes" votes. Most Republicans who voted did vote yes, but a sizable minority voted no, so it was not a unified party action. The claim also omits that 
the GOP-controlled state Senate acquitted him on all 16 articles tried
, with 
only two Republicans voting to remove him on any count
 (CBS News). The core fact, that Republican House members impeached a Republican, is accurate. "By his own party" overstates it by implying a party-wide act, and it ignores the acquittal.

The claim also leaves out the date (2019) and the setting (a debate over custody and child-abuse law).

clusters.text: James Talarico's campaign has stopped actively planning events in the final stretch of the race.
clusters.verdict_basis: Talarico did stop appearing in person for about 12 days. CNN and NBC News reported that his last in-person Texas event was Sept. 26. The Dallas Morning News reported that at least two events were scrapped: an Oct. 5 event for Black voters and an Oct. 6 Austin fundraiser. The campaign said the cause was the flu. It said he had held 100+ public events and would return soon. His calendar showed no candidate appearances, only canvassing, phone banks and get-out-the-vote gatherings (Townhall, Hot Air). The claim goes further than this. It says the campaign "stopped actively planning events in the final stretch." But the campaign kept scheduling field events. It also kept a CNN/Jubilee town hall set for Oct. 14. By Oct. 14, CNN reported he had returned to public events over the weekend, including Austin City Limits. The records back a temporary illness-related pause in his in-person appearances and some cancellations. They don't back a campaign-wide halt to event planning, so the claim as worded is misleading.
